topic: Day 1 · Variceal Bleeding II — When First-Line Fails
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Liver Unit & Portal Hypertension Service
speakerBio: A hepatologist who runs the acute liver bleed service. She teaches rescue therapy as a hierarchy of bridges and destinations — and the discipline never to confuse the two.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

Same unit, 40 minutes after a textbook first-line bundle. The Child–Pugh C patient banded an hour ago is vomiting fresh blood again; the NG aspirate is bright red, the BP is falling, and the endoscopist's second look shows blood welling from behind the bands faster than it can be cleared. First-line has failed. This session is the escalation ladder: how to buy time without killing the patient, and how modern rescue — the oesophageal stent and pre-emptive TIPS — has rewritten survival for the sickest bleeders.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

When banding fails, everything you do next is either a bridge (tamponade, stent) or the definitive pressure-drop (TIPS) — know which is which, and never let a bridge become the destination.

2 · Recognising failure of first-line control 🚩

Baveno VII defines failure to control bleeding within 5 days as any of: fresh haematemesis or ≥ 100 mL NG aspirate ≥ 2 h after treatment; hypovolaemic shock; or a 3 g/dL Hb fall in 24 h without transfusion. Once first-line (vasoactive drug + antibiotics + EVL) has failed, you are on the rescue ladder. Roughly 10–15% of acute variceal bleeds fail first-line — and mortality in this group is high, which is why the escalation must be fast and pre-planned.

3 · The escalation ladder — the master table 🪜

StepInterventionRoleKey limits
1Repeat endoscopy (re-band / glue)A second attempt at endoscopic control for a re-treatable lesionOnly if the anatomy is salvageable; not for torrential ongoing bleeding.
2Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore / Minnesota)Bridge — mechanical compression for hours only, to reach definitive therapyAirway MUST be protected (intubate). Max ~24 h. High complication rate.
3Self-expanding metal oesophageal stent (Danis / SX-ELLA)Better bridge — compresses varices, allows feeding, stays up to ~7–14 daysOesophageal varices only; migration risk; still a bridge to TIPS.
4TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt)Definitive pressure-drop — decompresses the portal systemEncephalopathy, heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension contraindicate.
💡 Memory hook — bridges vs the destination

Balloon and stent are bridges; TIPS is the destination. A balloon buys you hours, a stent buys you days — both exist only to get a bleeding patient alive to the definitive portal decompression of TIPS (or to a moment when the bleeding settles). Never leave a balloon up as a 'solution.'

4 · Balloon tamponade — the hours-only bridge 🎈

The Sengstaken–Blakemore tube (gastric + oesophageal balloons) and the Minnesota tube (adds an oesophageal aspiration port) tamponade varices by direct compression.

  • Airway first — always intubate before insertion. An unprotected airway with a balloon in a bleeding, often encephalopathic patient is a recipe for fatal aspiration.
  • Inflate the gastric balloon first (confirm position — imaging), apply gentle traction; inflate the oesophageal balloon only if bleeding continues, and only briefly.
  • Maximum ~24 hours — prolonged inflation causes pressure necrosis.
  • Complications: oesophageal rupture (catastrophic, from oesophageal balloon over-inflation or misplaced gastric balloon inflated in the oesophagus), aspiration pneumonia, mucosal necrosis, airway obstruction if the balloon migrates upward. Effective at temporary control (~80–90%) but rebleeds on deflation unless definitive therapy follows.
⚠️ Danger — the gastric balloon inflated in the oesophagus

The single most lethal balloon error: inflating the gastric balloon while it still sits in the oesophagus. This ruptures the oesophagus. Confirm the gastric balloon is below the diaphragm (aspirate gastric content, and confirm position radiologically) before full inflation. If the patient develops sudden pain or cardiovascular collapse during inflation, deflate immediately.

5 · Oesophageal stents — the better bridge 🩹

Self-expanding, removable, covered metal stents (Danis / SX-ELLA) are deployed across the bleeding oesophageal varices, tamponading them from within.

  • Advantages over the balloon: can stay in place up to ~7–14 days (vs 24 h), the patient can swallow/be fed, no continuous traction, lower rates of serious pressure complications.
  • Randomised data (Escorsell, Hepatology 2016) showed the stent achieved better bleeding control and fewer serious adverse events than balloon tamponade, though survival was similar — because both are bridges and survival depends on the definitive step.
  • Limits: for oesophageal varices only (not gastric); migration is the main problem; still fundamentally a bridge to TIPS or to spontaneous settling.

6 · TIPS — the definitive portal decompression ⚙️

A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt creates a channel through the liver parenchyma (jugular vein → hepatic vein → portal vein) held open by a covered stent, diverting portal blood into the systemic circulation and directly lowering portal pressure (target HVPG < 12 mmHg or a substantial reduction).

Pre-emptive (early) TIPS — the practice-changing concept

Rather than waiting for first-line to fail, pre-emptive ('early') TIPS is placed within 72 hours (ideally < 24 h) in high-risk patients who have been controlled by first-line therapy but are likely to fail. Baveno VII criteria for early TIPS:

  • Child–Pugh C (score < 14), or
  • Child–Pugh B with active bleeding at diagnostic endoscopy (despite vasoactive drug).

The landmark García-Pagán 'early TIPS' trial (NEJM 2010) and subsequent studies showed pre-emptive TIPS improved control of bleeding and survival in these high-risk patients versus standard drug + endoscopic therapy. This is the reason we now stratify risk at the index bleed and involve interventional radiology early — not only after failure.

Salvage (rescue) TIPS

When bridges are holding a failed first-line bleed, salvage TIPS is the definitive rescue. It controls bleeding in > 90% of refractory cases; outcome depends heavily on the severity of underlying liver disease.

🎯 Contrast — pre-emptive vs salvage TIPS

Pre-emptive/early TIPS: placed in a controlled high-risk patient (Child C < 14, or Child B with active bleeding) within 72 h to prevent the predicted failure — improves survival. Salvage TIPS: placed after first-line and bridges have failed to control an ongoing bleed — a rescue for a sicker, higher-mortality situation. The lesson of the last decade: move TIPS earlier in the highest-risk patient rather than waiting to be forced into it.

7 · Contraindications to TIPS ⛔

TIPS diverts portal blood past the liver, raises cardiac preload, and reduces first-pass hepatic clearance of gut nitrogen — its contraindications flow directly from that physiology:

  • Heart failure / severe tricuspid regurgitation — the shunt increases venous return and preload; a failing right heart cannot cope and decompensates.
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension (e.g. mean PAP > 45 mmHg / portopulmonary HTN) — increased flow into a high-resistance pulmonary bed precipitates right heart failure.
  • Overt / recurrent hepatic encephalopathy — bypassing the liver worsens encephalopathy by delivering unfiltered gut ammonia to the brain; uncontrolled HE is a (relative) contraindication.
  • Severe hepatic failure (e.g. bilirubin very high, MELD very high) — poor outcomes; and polycystic liver disease / hepatic malignancy along the tract, uncontrolled sepsis, unrelieved biliary obstruction are anatomical/physiological blocks.
💡 Pearl — the three questions before TIPS

Ask: Can the right heart take more preload? Are the lungs able to accept more flow? Is the brain already struggling (encephalopathy)? A 'no' to any of these is a red flag for TIPS — heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension and refractory encephalopathy are the classic contraindications.

8 · Gastric varices — a different beast 🎯

Gastric varices bleed less often than oesophageal but more severely, and band ligation is usually not the answer.

  • Cyanoacrylate ('glue') injection is first-line endoscopic therapy for bleeding gastric varices (especially fundal/GOV2/IGV1) — the glue polymerises on contact with blood and obliterates the varix. Risk: glue embolisation (pulmonary/systemic).
  • BRTO / BATO — balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (and its antegrade variant, BATO) — an interventional-radiology technique that occludes the gastrorenal/portosystemic shunt feeding the gastric varix and scleroses it retrogradely. Particularly useful for large fundal varices with a spontaneous shunt, and it does not raise encephalopathy risk the way TIPS can (it may even reduce it) — though it can worsen ascites/oesophageal varices by raising portal pressure.
  • TIPS is also effective for gastric varices and is chosen when portal decompression is otherwise needed; TIPS and BRTO are complementary, chosen by anatomy and comorbidity.

9 · The escalation walkthrough ⏱️

  1. Confirm failure (Baveno criteria) and get IR and the hepatologist on the phone now.
  2. Protect the airway — intubate before any balloon.
  3. Bridge: balloon tamponade for immediate torrential bleeding or place a covered oesophageal stent if available and expertise allows.
  4. Definitive: arrange salvage TIPS (or, if this is the index bleed in a high-risk patient controlled by first-line, pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h).
  5. For gastric varices: cyanoacrylate glue ± BRTO/TIPS by anatomy.
  6. Screen for and treat contraindications to TIPS (echo for RH function/pulmonary pressures, assess encephalopathy).
☠️ M&M — "The balloon was up for eighteen hours"

A 61-year-old Child–Pugh C man rebled after banding overnight. A Sengstaken tube was placed without intubation by an exhausted team because 'he was still talking.' Bleeding slowed. Over the night no one arranged TIPS — the balloon was treated as the treatment. At 18 hours he aspirated, desaturated, and on transfer for a belated TIPS was found to have an oesophageal perforation from the prolonged, over-traction'd balloon. He died of mediastinitis and respiratory failure. Errors: (1) no airway protection before balloon insertion in an encephalopathic bleeder; (2) the bridge became the destination — definitive TIPS was never mobilised; (3) the balloon stayed up far beyond the safe window, causing pressure necrosis and perforation. Lesson: intubate before the balloon, treat the balloon as a countdown clock of a few hours only, and the moment it goes up you should already be arranging the definitive portal decompression. A modern oesophageal stent would also have been a safer bridge.

10 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Failure of first-line (Baveno: rebleed / shock / 3 g Hb drop) puts you on the rescue ladder — escalate fast, call IR early.
  • Balloon tamponade = an hours-only bridge; always intubate first; max ~24 h; beware oesophageal rupture and aspiration.
  • Oesophageal stent (Danis) = a better, days-long bridge that allows feeding — but still a bridge.
  • Pre-emptive/early TIPS within 72 h for Child C < 14 or Child B with active bleeding — improves survival (García-Pagán, NEJM 2010). Salvage TIPS for failed bridges.
  • Gastric varices: cyanoacrylate glue first-line; BRTO/BATO or TIPS by anatomy.
  • TIPS contraindications: heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, overt/refractory encephalopathy (and severe hepatic failure) — ask: can the heart, lungs and brain tolerate the shunt?

Next session: we leave the cirrhotic and the ulcer behind for the 'other' upper GI bleeds — the tears, the hidden arteries, and the one you must never miss.

moderatorQs.q: Which patients qualify for pre-emptive (early) TIPS under Baveno VII, and what is the evidence that it helps?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Pre-emptive TIPS is placed within 72 hours (ideally < 24 h) of the index variceal bleed in patients at high risk of failing standard therapy, even though first-line has controlled the bleed. The Baveno VII high-risk criteria are: Child–Pugh C with a score < 14, or Child–Pugh B with active bleeding seen at diagnostic endoscopy despite a vasoactive drug. The landmark evidence is García-Pagán's early-TIPS RCT (NEJM 2010), which showed that placing a covered TIPS early in these high-risk patients improved control of bleeding and, crucially, survival compared with continued drug plus endoscopic therapy, without an unacceptable excess of encephalopathy. This reframed practice from 'TIPS only when everything fails' to 'stratify at the index bleed and shunt the sickest early.'

moderatorQs.q: Balloon tamponade and oesophageal stents are both called 'bridges.' Contrast them and explain the safety principles.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both are temporising measures to control a refractory oesophageal variceal bleed until definitive therapy (usually TIPS). Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore/Minnesota) works by direct compression, is effective in ~80–90%, but is an hours-only device — maximum ~24 h before pressure necrosis — with serious risks of oesophageal rupture and aspiration, and it mandates prior intubation. The self-expanding covered metal stent (Danis) is a better, days-long bridge: it tamponades from within, can stay up to ~7–14 days, allows the patient to swallow and be fed, and causes fewer serious adverse events (Escorsell, Hepatology 2016). The cardinal principle for both: they are bridges, not destinations — the moment either is deployed, the definitive portal decompression (TIPS) or a plan for settling must already be in motion, and the airway must be protected before a balloon.

moderatorQs.q: A Child C patient with refractory variceal bleeding has an echo showing severe pulmonary hypertension and recurrent encephalopathy. What does this mean for TIPS?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both findings are contraindications to TIPS, and together they make it hazardous. TIPS diverts portal blood into the systemic circulation, which increases venous return and cardiac preload and pushes more flow into the pulmonary bed — in severe pulmonary hypertension (e.g. mean PAP > ~45 mmHg) this can precipitate acute right heart failure. And because the shunt bypasses hepatic clearance of gut-derived ammonia, it worsens hepatic encephalopathy; recurrent/refractory HE is a further contraindication. So this patient sits in a very difficult space: TIPS is relatively contraindicated on two counts (plus heart-failure physiology), yet salvage options are limited. Management would lean on bridging (stent), optimising the encephalopathy and pulmonary pressures if at all possible, and an honest multidisciplinary discussion including prognosis and, where appropriate, ceilings of care — because forcing a TIPS here risks fatal right-heart or neurological decompensation.

audienceQs.q: What is the single most important safety step before inserting a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Protect the airway first — intubate. A patient bleeding torrentially from varices, frequently encephalopathic, cannot protect their own airway, and a balloon device sitting across the oesophagogastric junction dramatically increases the risk of fatal aspiration and can migrate upward to obstruct the airway. Beyond intubation, the other critical step is confirming the gastric balloon is below the diaphragm before full inflation (aspirate gastric content and confirm position radiologically) — inflating the gastric balloon while it is still in the oesophagus causes oesophageal rupture. Then apply gentle traction, keep the tube up for the shortest possible time (hours, max ~24 h), and have the definitive plan (TIPS) already moving. The balloon is a countdown clock, not a treatment.

audienceQs.q: How do I manage bleeding gastric varices differently from oesophageal ones?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Gastric varices are managed differently because band ligation is usually ineffective/unsafe for them. First-line endoscopic therapy for bleeding gastric (especially fundal, GOV2/IGV1) varices is cyanoacrylate 'glue' injection, which polymerises on contact with blood and obliterates the varix (watch for glue embolisation). For large fundal varices fed by a gastrorenal shunt, interventional radiology offers BRTO (balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration) or its antegrade variant BATO, which occludes and scleroses the varix via the shunt and — unlike TIPS — does not worsen (and may improve) encephalopathy, though it can aggravate ascites and oesophageal varices. TIPS remains an option, particularly where broader portal decompression is needed. The choice among glue, BRTO and TIPS is driven by the varix anatomy, the presence of a spontaneous shunt and the patient's encephalopathy/comorbidity profile.

audienceQs.q: Why does TIPS make hepatic encephalopathy worse?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because TIPS deliberately creates a portosystemic shunt — a channel that lets portal (gut) blood bypass the liver and flow straight into the systemic circulation. Normally the liver performs 'first-pass' clearance of nitrogenous products absorbed from the gut, principally converting ammonia to urea. When a large fraction of portal blood is shunted past functioning hepatocytes, gut-derived ammonia and other neurotoxins reach the brain unfiltered, precipitating or worsening hepatic encephalopathy — a recognised complication in a meaningful minority of TIPS patients. This is exactly why overt or recurrent encephalopathy is a contraindication to TIPS, and why post-TIPS patients are often managed with lactulose ± rifaximin. It is also why BRTO, which does not divert blood past the liver, can be preferable for gastric varices in an encephalopathy-prone patient.
